messages.subject: Discarded Observations
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am getting a warning message about missing (observational) covariate
data when I run my occupancy models, and it's baffling me as to why.
I imagine it's an easy fix, but I need a second set of eyes to see my
problem.

For the site covariates, my data set has 6 habitat types that are
incorporated as 5 indicator variables (0,1).  These habitat types
affect both occupancy and detection, and occu() has no problem
creating this model:

fm3 <- occu(~AV + Fynbos + Grass + NKB + SKB ~AV + Fynbos + Grass +
NKB + SKB, unmarked.dat)

For the observational/survey-specific covariates, I have one indicator
variable of whether or not it is breeding season (I'm looking at bird
data), and another variable indicating year (90, 91, or 92).  When I
run a model that includes either or both of these survey-specific
variables:
fm4 <- occu(~AV + Fynbos + Grass + NKB + SKB + j ~AV + Fynbos + Grass
+ NKB + SKB, unmarked.dat)

I get the following warning message, and the estimates do not match
Presence:
Warning messages:
1: In .local(umf, ...) :
  Some observations have been discarded because corresponding
covariates were missing.FALSE
2: In .local(umf, ...) :
  47 sites have been discarded because of missing data.FALSE

(Yes, a data set that includes multiple seasons and/or multiple years
should be looked at using a multi-season model, but I am just playing
around with the models to start and so am sticking to the simpler
models to get a better feel for the data structures/ error messages,
etc.)

The same data and model does run in Presence without any (visible)
errors.  And looking at the rows/sites that are discarded in occu(),
there is no apparent missing data.

Thank you for any help!  And thank you for creating the "unmarked"
pacakage!

~Kristin

Kristin Broms
Pre-doctoral Candidate
Quantitative Ecology and Resource Management
University of Washington
Seattle, WA 98195

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kristin,

Could you post the results of:

summary(unmarked.dat)

and maybe:

show(unmarked.dat)

Also, it sounds like you coded the dummy variables by hand, which is
unnecessary. It's much easier and less error prone to import the data
with a single column for habitat type. R will treat this as a factor
with a level for each habitat type and you could use:

occu(~habitat.type ~habitat.type, unmarked.dat)

Hope this helps,
Richard

Hello everyone,

I just submitted version 0.8-7 of unmarked to CRAN. It will probably
take a few days before it is available, but once it is, you can
download it from within R by typing install.packages("unmarked").
There are many minor changes in this version that can be browsed at
www.github.com/rbchan/unmarked <http://www.github.com/rbchan/unmarked>. The one major change is the addition
of a new function called gmultmix that fits a general
multinomial-mixture model to data collected during primary and
secondary sampling periods. This allows you to estimate abundance
while accounting for the probability that an individual will be
available for detection, and the probability of detection given
availability. Each of these three parameters can be modeled as linear
functions of covariates. The backbone of this function was provided by
Andy Royle who is now a co-developer. See the help page for more
details.

Ian Fiske who deserves most of the credit for developing this package
has unfortunately gotten a job. I suppose it's a good thing for him
but we will miss his help. Until he is able to return to the project,
I will be maintaining it. As always, send questions and bug reports to
the list.

Richard

in area sampled.  I suspect this term is in fact not accounting for
sampling effort as I had hoped.  Does anyone have any insights or
recommendations on how to account for variation in sampling area per
site?

Thanks for your assistance.

Matt

messages.subject: unmarkedFrames
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I thought I would provide a brief discussion of unmarkedFrames since
they have been the subject of several questions. Many users of R will
be accustomed to using data.frames to supply data to fitting functions
like glm. We decided against this approach for several reasons. First,
wildlife survey data are often associated with metadata that should be
linked to the data, not supplied as arguments to the fitting
functions. Second, we wanted to write custom methods (eg, show,
summary, plot, hist, etc...) for each unmarkedFrame type. Third, R
provides an object-oriented programming style know as S4 that makes it
easy to do the first two things. However, manipulating S4 objects may
not be straight-forward to some, so here is an example that should
provide some guidance. I will eventually clarify these things in the
documentation. For now, see help("unmarkedFrame-class")

# Import
wt <- read.csv(system.file("csv", "widewt.csv", package = "unmarked"))

# Set-up
y <- wt[, 2:4]
siteCovs <- wt[, c("elev", "forest", "length")]
obsCovs <- list(date = wt[, c("date.1", "date.2", "date.3")], ivel =
wt[, c("ivel.1", "ivel.2", "ivel.3")])
wtUMF <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y = y, siteCovs = siteCovs, obsCovs = obsCovs)

# Summarize
head(wtUMF)
summary(wtUMF)

# Request the data dimensions
numY(wtUMF)
numSites(wtUMF)
obsNum(wtUMF)

# Extract the y matrix
y <- getY(wtUMF)

# Extract the site covariates as a data.frame
sc <- siteCovs(wtUMF)

# standardize elevation (this could also be done in the formula)
sc$elev <- scale(sc$elev)
siteCovs(wtUMF) <- sc

# Extract the observation covariates as a data.frame in the long format
ocl <- obsCovs(wtUMF)

# Standardize date (this could be done in the formula)
ocl$date <- scale(ocl$date)
obsCovs(wtUMF) <- ocl

# Extract the observation covariates as a list of matrices
oc <- obsCovs(wtUMF, matrices=TRUE)

# Select data from the first 5 sites of the unmarkedFrame
subUMF <- wtUMF[1:5,]

# Select the first survey period
wtUMF1 <- wtUMF[,1]

These are the preferred ways of manipulating unmarkedFrames. If you
want to look at the underlying structure of the data use str:

str(wtUMF)

Note that each component of the object is in a "slot" and slots can be
extracted using the "@" operator.

slotNames(wtUMF)
wtUMF@y     # It's better to use getY(wtUMF)

I hope this helps,
Richard

occu function, were I am using only AIC as a selection criteria. With

these methods to use and also if you would suggest other methods to
use in the a stepwise selection procedure, so I don't end up with
nonsense models in my model list?

Thank you very much for your help,
Richard

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Stepwise selection criteria
messages.body_plain:
hi Richard -- I'm curious as to why you have these huge betas and SEs.
This suggests that the optimizer is not finding a stable optimum, its
diverging, which could be a result of poor starting values, poor
scaling of the covariates, or a basic non-identifiability. I think you
need to understand whats going on there.  That said, I'm curious as to
why those situations would appear to be better models. My intuition is
that if the optimizer does something stupid then it should get stuck
in a bad part of the parameter space and return a worse likelihood
(and hence AIC).  It might be useful if you could send me your data
file/R script which shows an example of this problem.

Now for your question: I think AIC should be a fine model-selection
metric, in general. I forget which criteria are used in the existing
selection procedures in R, Mallows Cp is one of them, but there are
many more. I suggest looking into that (the MASS library might have
some general functions for doing model selection which you could work
off of).

I think if you add factors based on significant coefficients at the
0.05 level then such factors will also show at least 2 units
improvement in AIC so there is a general consistency in how those two
methods should work, at least for the marginal "step" in the model
selection procedure.  However , if you are using small p-values to
select , simultaneously, a bunch of covariates then you could well
wind up with different models at the end.

No model selection method is generally better or worse than any other
(which is why there are so many).

regards
andy

good, and hence the lower AIC. Try using predict to see what your

to the user to ensure that the models are nested. Try this:

example(modSel)
LRT(fm1, fm2)

You should probably think about adjusting your p-values if you are
going to use this approach for model selection.

Richard
